subject: research/interval-scores
professional: a forecast-verification statistician (Gneiting/Raftery school) who refereed proper-scoring-rule papers; first checks the interval score formula and its closed-form expectation, then the novelty against Gneiting & Raftery 2007 and the repo's own interval-elicitation, then the detection-power arithmetic

evidence.correctness: Recomputed with a scipy/numpy script that does not import interval_scores: optimal score 4phi(z)/alpha at alpha 0.5/0.1/0.01 (matches to 1e-14), scale-misreport regrets 0.5189/0.1516/0.5961, shift regret 2.3237 vs quadratic 2.0627, Cauchy regret 1.36099 and 1.18047 by quadrature, detection n 20.15 and 328 by 4M-draw Monte Carlo (reported 20.1, 326.2), coverage n 290/467/133. All agree. The Winkler formula matches Gneiting & Raftery 2007. One correctness failure is of method rather than arithmetic: detection_n (model.py:111) is a 50%-power sample size while coverage_n (:117) is ~95%-power, yet section 5 compares them.
evidence.completeness: README claims: strict propriety, closed-form regret for normal and Cauchy, exact optimal score, level-dependent asymmetry, Cauchy bounded paired differences. All present in code and results. Ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py | diff - experiments/results.txt`: identical. 7 tests ran OK in 0.76 s. Bounded variant explicitly not developed (stated limit). figure.py exists, not run beyond reading.
evidence.verification: 7 tests pass. 6 hand-seeded mutations: 4 caught, 2 survived: detection_n z*z -> z (model.py:111, a headline output of section 5, no test) and the binomial variance term in coverage_n (:117). The only coverage_n test asserts the result is > 0, so mutation (a-b)**2 -> (a-b) was caught only by a sign flip, not by magnitude. paired_moments variance is checked nowhere. Core regret and score formulas are well tested against quadrature (that part would catch real bugs).
evidence.craft: Read model.py, tests, run.py. Stdlib only, short, readable, docstrings with the derivation. Defects: no input validation (alpha outside (0,1), l>u, p outside (0,1) for quantile, kind other than 'cauchy' silently treated as normal); optimal_score ignores kind and silently gives the normal answer; normal quantile by 200-step bisection on [-40,40] rather than erfinv; paired_moments is a 240k-point pure-Python Simpson loop per call; tests check sums to 3 decimals only.
evidence.claims: Section 2-4 numbers are backed by results.txt and reproduce. Failed: section 5 'score sees width errors much faster than coverage count' compares unlike powers and an undefined 'comparable' miscalibration (lam=0.85 needs 326 tasks, more than coverage n=290 at true 0.05). Novelty: abstract presents the Winkler regret closed form and finite Cauchy paired difference as findings, but interval-elicitation already states exact Winkler regret finite for Cauchy; section 6 discloses the companion relationship but the README does not. Disclaimer/limits section present. 'Strictly proper' is textbook (Gneiting & Raftery 2007).
evidence.fitness: A researcher could build on the closed forms and the practical rule (compare reports by paired differences), but there is no real-data check, no named venue, and the drift scenario (verifier drift tolerance) is a modelling assumption not tied to any dataset. Nearest prior work: Gneiting & Raftery 2007 (interval score, propriety), Gneiting 2011 (quantiles as optimal point forecasts), Bracher et al. 2021 (WIS), and this repo's interval-elicitation. The new parts are small: level-dependent narrow/wide asymmetry table and detection-n tables. Below the PhD+ programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md (no programme, no real data, no artefact a practitioner adopts).
evidence.domain: A verification statistician would accept the score and the propriety argument; they would object that the closed form E S*=4 s phi(z)/alpha is a known textbook identity (G&R 2007 eq. for normal), that detection power is inconsistent, that the Cauchy 'no mean' claim for scores is fine but unemphasised as standard (Cauchy has no mean, so any unbounded-loss score fails), and that Wald-type coverage_n at small n is approximate with no continuity correction.

defects.what: Detection-n comparison uses 50% power for the score test (detection_n z^2) and ~95% power for the coverage test (coverage_n z+z), so the whitepaper section 5 conclusion that the score detects faster is not like for like (about 4x factor on the score side)
Novelty overstated: Winkler regret closed form and finite-Cauchy paired result already in research/interval-elicitation; README does not say so
detection_n and coverage_n (headline section 5 outputs) have no test of their values; mutations survived or were caught only by sign
No input validation; optimal_score ignores kind and silently returns the normal answer for Cauchy; unknown kind treated as normal

verdict: The mathematics is correct: every headline number (optimal score, misreport regrets, shift curvature, Cauchy regrets, detection n, coverage n) recomputed independently, and experiments/run.py reproduces results.txt exactly. It does not meet the bar: claims is 2 because the section 5 detection-vs-coverage comparison mixes 50% and 95% power and novelty over interval-elicitation and Gneiting & Raftery 2007 is overstated, and verification is 2 because 2 of 6 seeded mutations survived, both in the detection-sample-size functions. As research it is a competent but small exercise on a known score, with no real data. Median is 2.
